meta.title: Boosting Sentinel-2 Crop Disease Classification via Self-Supervised Pretraining: A Comparative Study of CNN and SwinV2 Backbones

abstract: Satellite imagery can deliver timely, scalable insights to farmers and cooperatives, enabling early detection of crop stress and disease before symptoms become evident at field level. Motivated by the Beyond Visible Spectrum AI for Agriculture 2026 Kaggle challenge, we investigated a practical end-to-end pipeline that converts raw multi-spectral Sentinel-2 patches into actionable disease-class predictions. The task consists of classifying four categories (Aphid, Blast, Rice Plant Hopper (RPH), Rust) from per-band Geo- TIFF inputs (B1–B12). To assess design choices under class imbalance and acquisition variability, we perform a controlled comparison between a convolutional backbone and a hierarchical Transformer backbone, and evaluate the impact of self-supervised masked pretraining on downstream performance. Models are fine-tuned with class-weighted crossentropy. Finally, we leveraged an Explainable AI technique to attribute predictions to spatial regions and spectral bands, supporting the interpretability of the architectures. Results show that self-supervised pretraining can improve classification performance, with clearer gains for the SwinV2 backbone than for ResNet-18. Explainability analysis qualitatively confirms that the architecture considered focuses on specific regions of the field, taking its decisions with varying degrees of confidence (the self-supervised-initialised one is more confident). Furthermore, this analysis shows how the best-performing net focuses on the relevant agronomic bands. Potential limits of the study so far conducted and further research directions are illustrated in the Discussion section.

blocks.html: Satellite Earth observation enables large-scale, repeatable monitoring of vegetation conditions and has become a valuable source of information for crop stress and disease assessment [1, 2]. Sentinel-2 multi-spectral imagery is particularly relevant in this context, as its spectral bands can capture biochemical and structural changes in the canopy that are often associated with plant health variations [3].

Recent studies have demonstrated that Sentinel-2 can support the detection of disease or pest-related phenomena, including wheat yellow rust and cotton aphid infestation [4, 5], and that deep models can leverage multi-spectral series to mitigate confounding effects such as phenology and management practices. However, practical deployment remains limited by the scarcity and imperfect nature of ground-truth labels [6], especially when the target is a fine-grained discrimination between visually and spectrally similar stressors [7]. Motivated by the Beyond Visible Spectrum AI for Agriculture 2026 Kaggle challenge [8], this work focused on a challenging fine-grained classification task with four disease/pest categories (Aphid, Blast, Rust, RPH), very well known problems among farmers addressed also in previous works (e.g. [9]). The competition dataset is relatively small and markedly imbalanced, reflecting a realistic constraint in agricultural monitoring where collecting balanced, high-quality annotations at scale is expensive. In this setting, standard supervised training is prone to overfitting and poor minority-class generalization [10]. To address this limitation, we investigated self-supervised learning (SSL) via masked image modeling as a principled way to exploit additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery for representation learning prior to supervised fine-tuning [11, 12]. We conducted a controlled comparison between a convolutional backbone (ResNet-18) [13] and a hierarchical Transformer backbone (SwinV2) [14], evaluating each architecture with and without SSL pretraining under consistent training and evaluation protocols. By doing so, we quantify when and how SSL improves performance across backbone families. Prior work on Sentinel-2 disease and pest monitoring has largely relied on tailored spectral indices or classical classifiers (like Random Forest Algorithms) applied to individual stressors, such as wheat yellow rust [4] and cotton aphid infestation [5]. In parallel, masked image modelling and other self-supervised strategies have been explored for satellite imagery, but mostly as general-purpose foundation models [11] or for tasks such as land-cover segmentation and classification [15], and on other acquisition platforms such as multi-spectral UAV data [16], rather than for fine-grained crop disease classification from Sentinel-2. To the best of our knowledge, the specific combination of masked self-supervised pretraining, fine-grained disease/pest discrimination from Sentinel-2 patches, and a controlled comparison of convolutional and Transformer backbones under class imbalance and label scarcity [6] has not been systematically studied. Our contribution is therefore to empirically complement prior Sentinel-2 disease detection literature for operational crop health monitoring.

The dataset consists of 890 samples provided as a folder containing one GeoTIFF file per Sentinel-2 band (e.g., B1.tif, geospatial raster format that stores pixel values together with georeferencing metadata, enabling reproducible access across common GIS and scientific toolchains. In this challenge, we treated each folder as a single multi-spectral patch (no temporal aggregates, just uncorrelated snapshots) and load the bands in a fixed order (B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B8A, B9, B11, B12), producing a 12-channel tensor.

blocks.html: Sentinel-2 MSI bands span visible, near-infrared (NIR), and shortwave infrared (SWIR) wavelengths and have different native spatial resolutions. Since the geometrical resolution varies across bands, each band is read as float32 and resampled to a common spatial grid in order to feed a single backbone with a fixed input shape. Specifically, we resized each band to 256 × 256 pixels (holding 10 meters per pixel side) using bilinear interpolation, and stack them along the channel axis to obtain X ∈R12×256×256. Multispectral inputs exhibit heterogeneous ranges across bands and acquisitions, so a per-band standard scaling normalization (at the moment stats coming not from all the unlabeled dataset but just from the labeled one, next steps will involve also a careful descriptive analysis of the unlabeled dataset) was performed to improve optimization stability. It is important to notice that at this preliminary stage of the work no cloud-masking algorithms have been employed, all the patches refer to Bottom Of Atmosphere (BOA) reflectance and have been recovered using the well-known Sen2Cor ESA algorithm[17].

All pipelines share the same data preprocessing aforementioned. We focused here on the methodological comparison between backbone architectures and training regimes, under a precise control protocol. For each backbone, we compared a purely supervised baseline against a self-supervised (SSL) initialization followed by supervised fine-tuning so yielding four configurations. Table 1 summarizes the key hyperparameters shared across all runs. As convolutional baseline we chose ResNet-18 (11 million parameters) since it is a widely adopted architecture for visual recognition. To let the architecture ingest multi-spectral inputs, the first convolution is modified to accept C = 12 channels instead of RGB.

As a Transformer baseline, we chose Swin Transformer V2 [14, 18] (27 million parameters), which builds hierarchical multi-scale representations using shifted-window attention and is known for its ability to identify complex patterns. Similarly to the CNN case, we adapt the input projection (patch embedding) to accept 12 channels, keeping the downstream Transformer stages unchanged. To leverage unlabeled data we pretrained each backbone using masked image modeling in the spirit of SimMIM [12, 19]. The unlabeled dataset consists of about 120 GB of Sentinel-2 agricultural patches (always available through Kaggle Competition website in the same format .tif abovementioned) taken all around the world (note that a geographical independence between the unlabelled and labelled dataset had not been assessed properly so at this stage of the work overlaps between the two datasets can occur) and, unlike the labeled one, providing also the information about the acquisition date (basically for the same area, 4 different temporal snapshots have been taken, one per season). In particular, given an input tensor, we randomly masked a fraction ρ of non-overlapping 32 × 32 pixel regions (mask ratio ρ = 0.6), setting those regions to zero. The encoder received only the partially observed tensor Xmask, where masked areas are removed and visible areas remain unchanged. The encoder outputs latent feature maps, which are passed through a lightweight reconstruction head that projects them back to the original multi-spectral space, producing a reconstruction ˆX with the same dimensionality as X. The objective is to predict the original pixel values in the masked regions.
We therefore minimized an L1 reconstruction loss computed exclusively over masked pixels [12]:

blocks.html: ⊙denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product, and ϵ ensures numerical stability. This formulation prevents the model from trivially copying visible pixels and forces it to learn spatial and spectral correlations [19] in order to infer the missing content. In Figure 1, checkpoints of reconstructions produced during training are presented. After pretraining, the reconstruction head is discarded and only the encoder weights are retained to initialize supervised fine-tuning. For supervised learning, we attached a classification head to each backbone and optimize standard cross-entropy over the four classes. We addressed class imbalance by using a weighted cross-entropy loss, where each class k is assigned a weight wk inversely related to its frequency in the training split. This encourages the optimizer to penalize mistakes on under-represented categories more strongly and improves balanced performance (macro-F1) across classes [10]. All configurations were fine-tuned under the same optimization setup to ensure as fair a comparison as possible, considering that the fine-tuning operations would have taken much more computational time and resources. We used the AdamW optimizer with cosine annealing scheduling. Since the problem presents strong unbalancing (for the Rust class just 40 samples have been provided) the performance of the model was evaluated by 3 separate runs with different random seeds producing 3 different 80%-20% train-val splits [20].

blocks.html: Figure 2 summarizes the main comparison across the four configurations. Overall, self-supervised initialization consistently affected downstream performance, and the magnitude of the gain depended on the chosen backbone. In addition, the transformer backbone exhibited stronger performance than the CNN baseline in our setting, suggesting benefits from hierarchical attention and multi-scale modeling on multi-spectral patches (previously these improvements had been proven only on general downstream tasks [15]). However, it is important to notice that this claim should be better proved in future work (under a proper capacity-matched comparison protocol) since also other key elements (e.g. parameters, latent embedding size[21]) of the two architectures vary significantly. Beyond overall scores, SSL can change optimization behavior. Figure 3 reports validation curves comparing supervised training from Random initialization against SSL initialization (shown for a representative backbone). SSL pretraining typically accelerated convergence across epochs [16], indicating more stable representations before fine-tuning [12]. For the sake of completeness, Figure 4 shows the comparison of confusion matrices for the best-performing configuration on the validation split. By inspection, it is worth noticing firstly the big difference between randomly initialised SwinV2 (Figure 4a) architecture and the SSL-initialised one (Figure 4b); secondly, one may notice a marked imbalance between classes just by looking at the main diagonal.

Beyond predictive performance, interpretability is particularly relevant in agronomic applications [22], where practitioners benefit from understanding why a model assigns a given disease category. We adopted two complementary explainability approaches: (i) a perturbation-based band ablation analysis to quantify the contribution of each Sentinel-2 band to the prediction, and (ii) the gradient-based method SmoothGrad to obtain visually stable spatial saliency maps[23]. These techniques were applied on a completely new patch provided, according to the standard required by the Neural Net, by an Italian agritech company TERRAVIONICS [24] through proprietary software and pipelines. The new patch depicts an area near Korla, central Xinjiang, acquired during the cotton boll period, a phase for which severe aphid infestation in this district is documented in the literature [5]. In this case the SSL- SwinV2 model predicts with 95.9% of confidence the presence of Aphid (it is worth remarking the confidence of the net could differ significantly from the accuracy, in future works this assessment can be carried out leveraging tools like reliability diagrams). In terms of band ablation we start from a given input tensor X ∈RC×H×W and predicted class k. We measure the importance of band c by replacing that band with a baseline value (here 0, corresponding to the neutral value in the normalized input space) and simply observe the drop in model confidence ∆c(X) and the shifting in class prediction (marked with red bar). Larger positive values of this ∆indicate that band c provides stronger evidence for the current prediction, while values close to zero suggest limited contribution. Conversely, negative values (∆c < 0, slightly noticeable for Band 9) mean that replacing band c with the baseline increases the confidence, suggesting that band c provides evidence against class k for that sample (or introduces confounding information/noise). This yields a per-sample spectral importance profile (reported in Figure 5). From inspecting the ablation plot, we expect that additional performance gains are achievable. In particular, for some samples, completely removing specific bands results in an increase in the model confidence for the predicted class, i.e., those bands act as inhibitory or confounding evidence rather than supportive cues for the net (see the B9). At the same time, the ablation profile indicates that the current SSL-initialized Net is already learning meaningful spectral information, since the most influential channels are B8, B6, and B3, which are consistent with bands commonly associated with vegetation condition and Aphid sensitivity as explained in [5]. Taken together, these observations suggest a dual message: SSL pretraining is effective in initializing classifiers backbone letting them identify the relevant and physically consistent spectral drivers, yet the learned representation is still relatively coarse and can likely be improved by refining some key factor like pre-training strategy. Proceeding with the analysis, to obtain spatially stable saliency maps, we applied SmoothGrad by averaging input gradients over N = 200 Gaussian-perturbed samples, with ϵi ∼N(0, σ2) (perturbation) and σ = 0.4 in the normalized input space. A global spatial saliency map was then obtained by summing absolute attributions across spectral bands. For visualisation, the aggregated map is overlaid on a pseudo-RGB composite (B4, B3, B2) as presented in Figure 6. As shown in Figure 1 the SSL-initialized net is trained to reconstruct masked blocks of the images, this can have influenced the net in producing these visual artefacts. However, it is difficult to draw this conclusion with confidence since no hyperparameter tuning has been performed (so these artefacts can be produced by a strong self-supervised under-training as well). We expect to analyse these aspects in future works.

blocks.html: The proposed pipeline demonstrated that, for agricultural disease classification from Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, masked image modeling can effectively exploit abundant unlabeled data to enhance the performance of the classification backbone. In particular, this performance coming from SimMIM-style pretraining suggested that SSL initialization encourages the backbone to learn general-purpose spatial–spectral representations that transfer well under limited supervision, yielding more stable optimization and better macro-F1 score once combined with imbalance-aware fine-tuning.

Despite these strengths, our setting also presented limitations. First, each sample is time-independent, which prevents the model from exploiting temporal signatures that are often informative for stress progression and phenology [25]. Recent work on masked pretraining for temporal and multi-spectral satellite data suggests that explicitly modeling the time axis can further improve robustness and transfer across tasks [11]. Second, satellite-based classification is prone to domain shift across acquisitions (e.g., illumination, atmosphere, phenological stage, management practices), which can degrade performance when the deployment distribution differs from the training set [26]. Although the methodological novelty of the paper is intentionally limited, the study addresses a targeted gap: the role of self-supervised initialization in a constrained remote-sensing scenario characterized by few classes, class imbalance, and multi-spectral crop disease data. In this context, the contribution is primarily empirical: rather than proposing a new model, we provide controlled evidence on when SSL is beneficial and how its impact depends on the chosen backbone. The results suggest that SSL yields clearer improvements for the Transformer-based architecture than for the convolutional baseline. This point should not be overstated, and further ablation would be required to validate the hypothesis; nevertheless, the observed difference indicates that the usefulness of SSL should not be treated as architecture-independent in crop disease classification from Sentinel-2 imagery. These considerations naturally motivate the future research directions of this work, which will focus not only on improving the efficiency of the SSL strategy and investigating the impact of increasing the amount and variability of training data (through the inclusion of additional multi-temporal and multi-conditional Sentinel-2 imagery) but also on varying the classification backbone structure. Finally, we aim at including a wider and more systematic XAI evaluation to boost interpretation of our results, considering additional techniques and more quantitative metrics.
